The final years of the Yuan dynasty were marked by struggle, famine, and bitterness among the populace. In time, the Yuan lost all influence in China. The reigns of the later Yuan emperors were short and marked by intrigues and rivalries. Uninterested in administration, they were separated from both the army and the populace, and China was torn by dissension and unrest. Outlaws ravaged the country without interference from the weakening Yuan armies. From the late 1340s onwards, people in the countryside suffered from frequent natural disasters such as droughts, floods and the resulting famines, and the government's lack of effective policy led to a loss of popular support. In 1351, the Red Turban Rebellion led by Song loyalists started and grew into a nationwide uprising and established a renewed Song dynasty in 1351 with its capital at Kaifeng. In 1354, when Toghtogha led a large army to crush the Red Turban rebels, Toghon Temür suddenly dismissed him for fear of betrayal. This resulted in Toghon Temür's restoration of power on the one hand and a rapid weakening of the central government on the other. He had no choice but to rely on local warlords' military power, and gradually lost his interest in politics and ceased to intervene in political struggles. He fled north to Shangdu from Khanbaliq in 1368 after the approach of the forces of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), founded by Zhu Yuanzhang in the south. Zhu Yuanzhang was a former commander in the army of the Red Turban Song dynasty and assumed power as Emperor after the death of the Red Turban Song Emperor Han Lin'er, who had tried to regain Khanbaliq, which eventually failed, and who died in Yingchang two years later (1370). Yingchang was seized by the Ming shortly after his death. The Prince of Liang, Basalawarmi established a separate pocket of resistance to the Ming in Yunnan and Guizhou, but his forces were decisively defeated by the Ming in 1381. By 1387 the remaining Yuan forces in Manchuria under Naghachu had also surrendered to the Ming dynasty.

Gian Galeazzo Visconti, elevated to duke of Milan in 1395, wielded unprecedented military and administrative skill: he subjugated Verona, Vicenza and Padua through masterful siegecraft, forged an efficient bureaucracy and legal code, and patronized great works such as the Certosa di Pavia and the Milan Cathedral, leaving a legacy of centralized power and early Renaissance statecraft. His sudden death in 1402, however, unleashed a destructive succession struggle: his son Gian Maria's cruel reign ended in assassination, and although Filippo Maria endeavored to replicate his father's triumphs, he died in 1447 without a male heir, fracturing the Visconti dominions. With Milan briefly declared a republic, the city's elite in 1450 invited Francesco Sforza - husband of Gian Galeazzo's granddaughter Bianca - to restore order. Sforza's accession marked both the culmination of Visconti political legacies and the extinction of their dynasty in Milan.

By the early 18th century, the Safavid Empire was collapsing under the weight of weak leadership, internal corruption, and mounting external threats. Shah Sultan Husayn's inability to manage religious tensions and defend the realm left Persia vulnerable to the Sunni Afghan Ghilzai tribe, who under Mahmud Hotak crushed a Safavid army at Gulnabad in 1722 and besieged Isfahan for seven months. Starvation and disease ravaged the capital until Husayn surrendered, ending over two centuries of Safavid rule. In the chaos that followed, the Ottomans and Russians seized border territories, while the Afghans' grip on central Persia proved unstable. Safavid prince Tahmasp II maintained a fragile rump state in the northeast, but it was clear that only a decisive military leader could reunite the fractured realm. That leader emerged in the form of Nadir Qoli Beg, a gifted commander from the Turkoman Afshar tribe. Rising from obscurity in Khorasan, Nadir allied with Tahmasp II in 1726, swiftly defeating the Afghan occupiers and reclaiming Isfahan. He reformed the Persian army, drove out Ottoman forces, and forced Russia to relinquish its Caspian conquests. Disillusioned by Tahmasp's political blunders, Nadir deposed him in 1732, ruling as regent for the young Abbas III before formally taking the throne in 1736 as Nadir Shah, founder of the Afsharid dynasty. His ascendance marked not only the restoration of Persian unity but also the beginning of an era of aggressive expansion, culminating in campaigns that would carry his armies from the Caucasus to Delhi.

When Karim Khan Zand rose to power in the mid-18th century, Persia was still reeling from decades of war and political fragmentation following the fall of the Safavids and the turbulent reign of Nadir Shah. Declaring himself not 'Shah' but Vakil ol-Ra'aya - 'Deputy of the People' - Karim Khan positioned his rule as one of service rather than autocracy. From his capital in Shiraz, he prioritised stability, justice, and economic revival. He reformed taxation to ease burdens on farmers and merchants, encouraged agricultural production, and restored security along trade routes, which revived commerce both internally and with foreign powers such as the British East India Company. His administration promoted religious tolerance, reduced sectarian tensions, and fostered a climate in which scholarship and the arts could flourish. Karim Khan's building projects transformed Shiraz into a vibrant political and cultural centre. He commissioned citadels, bazaars, mosques, gardens, and public baths, many of which became enduring symbols of the Zand era's prosperity. By curbing corruption, protecting property rights, and ensuring fair legal processes, he won a reputation as a just and approachable ruler. His nearly three-decade reign (1751-1779) brought an uncommon period of peace to much of Persia, allowing the country to recover from the devastation of previous decades. Though his successors could not maintain his legacy, Karim Khan's reforms left a lasting imprint on Persian governance and urban life, remembered as a rare moment of stability in an otherwise turbulent century.
The Centralizing Reforms of John II

Upon his accession in 1481, John II moved with calculated precision to restore the crown's supremacy: he convened the Cortes at Évora and compelled his vassals to swear a stringent oath of obedience, while reviving the beneplacet to bar any papal letters from publication without royal approval. He then stripped the great nobles of their feudal prerogatives, in turn dismantling aristocratic courts and centralizing legal authority in the monarchy. More dramatically, John accused both the Duke of Braganza (the premier noble of the realm) and the Duke of Viseu (his own cousin, and his wife's brother) of treason. Braganza was executed, and Viseu murdered by John personally. Simultaneously, John overhauled the royal finances - abolishing noble tax exemptions, curbing lavish court expenditures, and installing a professional bureaucracy to ensure steady revenue for the crown. These reforms not only crushed internal dissent but also replenished Portugal's coffers and underwrote a renewed surge of maritime exploration along Africa's coastline and towards India, cementing his legacy as the 'Perfect Prince' whose ruthless efficiency sparked an age of global expansion.

Long nominally under Novgorod's sway and paying tribute for centuries, the Komi principality of Great Perm along the upper Kama River maintained autonomy from its capital at Cherdyn until a steady Muscovite encroachment began under Vasily II, who in 1451 installed a loyal prince named Mikhail Yermolayevich. By 1471 Moscow had superseded Novgorod's claim, tightening its grip through tribute and political appointments, and in 1505 Ivan III formally abolished the Perm princely line - seizing Cherdyn, supplanting local elites, and folding Permia into the Grand Duchy of Moscow's expanding realm. This in turn ushered in the direct administration of Finno-Ugric territories by Moscow and marked a pivotal moment in her eastward consolidation.

The maritime republic of Ragusa secured its survival on the Adriatic by embracing a pragmatic vassalage to the Ottoman sultans from 1458 onward, paying an annual tribute in lieu of direct rule while retaining full internal autonomy and its Catholic identity. Ottoman sovereigns formalized this relationship through a series of capitulations - first granted by Murad II in the 1430s and codified under Süleyman the Magnificent - that guaranteed Ragusan merchants exceptionally low customs duties, freedom to trade throughout the empire, and protection as 'dhimmis' without personal poll-tax burdens. In return, Dubrovnik became a critical node in the 'Ragusa Road' - the main overland corridor linking Istanbul to Western Europe - facilitating not only commercial exchange but also diplomatic and cultural encounters across Rumelia. Though always balancing its ties to Venice and later the Habsburgs, Ragusa's layered allegiance to the Ottomans enabled the city state to flourish as a neutral broker.

Pir Muhammad was the son of Jahangir Mirza, Timur's favourite son and heir-designate until his early death in 1376. As various other uncles and brothers were either killed in battle or murdered during Timur's long reign, Pir Muhammad had managed to succeed his grandfather in 1405 - although without any real political or military support. A competent general, Pir Muhammad had led the Timurid vanguard into India in 1397 and ruled briefly as governor of Multan. However, following Timur's death he struggled to assemble allies across the Timurid Empire, and within two years had been overthrown by his cousin Khalil Sultan.

Khalil Sultan was the son of Miran Shah, a son of Timur who had been excluded from the succession for being hedonistic and mentally unstable. A favourite of his grandfather, Khalil Sultan distinguished himself during campaigns in India and Transoxiana during the early 1400s and overthrew his cousin Pir Muhammad in 1407 after seizing the royal treasury at Samarkand. Though an effective general, Khalil Sultan was easily led and relied heavily on low-born favourites to administer his territories, and his popularity waned following regional famines and perceived widespread corruption. Khalil Sultan's brief reign ended in May 1409, when his uncle Shâh Rûkh entered Samarkand unopposed and proclaimed himself Amir.

Conceived by Peter the Great and implemented by his successors Anna and Elizabeth, the Great Northern Expedition was a massive 18th century scientific and exploratory undertaking led by the Danish cartographer Vitus Bering. Beginning in 1733 and continuing for over a decade, the expedition aimed to map and explore the Russian Empire's vast eastern territories, particularly Siberia and the Russian Far East, in order to gain a better understanding of the region's geography, wildlife and indigenous peoples. The expedition achieved significant milestones, such as the discovery of the Bering Strait, which separates Asia from North America, and numerous new geographical and scientific findings. It played a pivotal role in expanding Russia's knowledge of its eastern lands and contributed to its claim on Alaska. The expedition, which was mammoth in both scope and cost, had a lasting impact on European exploration and scientific research.
